items.prompt: Explain why fictional Tano Meals’ customer survey and poster are not complete definitions of marketing. [6]
items.canonical_answer: The survey is market research, collecting information; the poster is advertising, communicating a promotional message. Marketing is the wider process identifying and anticipating wants and guiding how an offering meets them. Product, price and access decisions remain beyond those two activities.
marking_guidance: Error: The survey is market research, collecting information; the poster is advertising, communicating a promotional message.

items.prompt: Define a market. [2]
items.canonical_answer: A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a particular product or service. Contact can occur at a stall, through a shop, by telephone or online. Define what is being traded and the relevant buyers or area when comparing markets. A market is not the activity of marketing or merely the physical building where sales occur.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a particular product or service.

items.prompt: Define marketing. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Marketing is the management process which identifies consumer wants and anticipates their future wants. It supports decisions about the offering and how customers obtain it, not simply promotional communication. Research is one information-gathering activity within it. A business needs to connect identified wants with realistic product, price, promotion and access choices.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Marketing is the management process which identifies consumer wants and anticipates their future wants.

items.prompt: Explain how Omi can identify and meet its customers’ short-break needs. Fictional Omi Lunches learns that workers need portable meals collected quickly during a short break. [6]
items.canonical_answer: A business identifies customer needs through relevant research, sales patterns, feedback and observation. It then decides which customers to serve and designs a suitable product or service, price and access. A stated preference is not a guaranteed sale: affordability, competing products and the buying situation matter. Test a feasible offering and use feedback to improve it. Customer focus does not require accepting every request at any cost. A change must fit resources and earn sufficient revenue for the enterprise’s purpose. Customer needs can change, so an initial survey does not remove the need to review actual behaviour. A suitable response could combine secure packaging, a collection time and an affordable price, then review actual orders and complaints. Advertising the old slow service would not address the stated need.
marking_guidance: Starting point: A business identifies customer needs through relevant research, sales patterns, feedback and observation.

items.prompt: State two objectives of marketing. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Marketing objectives can include increasing sales, increasing market share, attracting new customers, retaining existing customers, developing awareness and supporting a successful new-product launch. They should fit wider business aims and available resources. State a result, not just an activity: running an advertisement is an action, whereas increasing awareness among a defined target group is an objective. A measurable target and time period make review possible. More sales are not automatically more profit if the cost of achieving them exceeds the added return.
marking_guidance: Point: Marketing objectives can include increasing sales, increasing market share, attracting new customers, retaining existing customers, developing awareness and supporting a successful new-product launch.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether Tula should target work-purpose buyers instead of fashion buyers. Fictional Tula Bags can make durable work bags in small batches. Interviews indicate mechanics need strong tool compartments, while fashion customers want frequent style changes that Tula cannot provide. [8]
items.canonical_answer: Market segmentation divides a market into groups of consumers with similar needs. The syllabus bases include product, region, purpose, price, age and gender. Segments can overlap: buyers in one region can also seek budget-priced products for a particular purpose. Use evidence that the chosen grouping affects needs rather than assuming all people in a demographic category behave alike. Assess potential demand, purchasing ability, competition, reach and whether the business can serve the segment with its resources. A small enterprise may focus on a niche instead of trying to offer everything to everyone, but excessive dependence on a narrow group creates risk. A supported target decision links a real need with an achievable offering and recognises the strongest alternative. Targeting work-purpose buyers fits its capability and the stated need better than the fashion alternative. Confirm sufficient paid demand and feasible price before committing; the word mechanic alone does not prove a profitable market.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Market segmentation divides a market into groups of consumers with similar needs.

items.prompt: Explain how product categories could help Uta organise its target offering. Fictional Uta Sports distinguishes buyers seeking footwear from buyers seeking sports equipment. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Product segmentation groups a wider market by the type or category of product sought. It can help a supplier focus its range and expertise, but a product label alone does not explain the customer need. Buyers within a category may still differ in price, use and preferred features. The categories can guide separate ranges and promotion. Further evidence is needed to choose the footwear features and price.

items.prompt: Explain how region can guide Oha’s stock choice without assuming identical buyers. Fictional Oha Clothing compares demand for warm outerwear in colder inland areas with demand in warmer locations. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Regional segmentation groups customers by geographical area. Climate, access, travel distance or local demand can make needs differ between areas. The grouping is useful when those differences affect the offering or delivery; it does not prove everyone in one area wants the same thing. Regional evidence can guide stock and delivery, while actual customer data should check the assumed climate-related need.

items.prompt: Explain how intended use can guide Teya’s bag features. Fictional Teya Bags distinguishes tool-carrying bags from small everyday leisure bags. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Purpose segmentation groups customers by the use they want from a product. The same broad product can serve school, work, travel or recreation, requiring different features. This can be more informative than a demographic label where function drives the purchase. A buyer can belong to different purpose segments for different occasions. Strength and internal compartments may matter for tools, while size and style may matter for leisure. Research should confirm those priorities before design.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Purpose segmentation groups customers by the use they want from a product.

items.prompt: Explain how price levels can help Kira distinguish its target offerings. Fictional Kira Furniture compares a simple low-priced desk with a more expensive customised range. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Price segmentation groups demand by price level or willingness and ability to pay, such as budget and premium ranges. The offering must deliver value the group recognises; a higher price label alone does not create superior quality or willing buyers. Low-price demand can require careful cost control, while a premium offer needs credible benefits. The budget group may value affordability, but the desk must still meet its basic purpose. Premium customers need a reason to accept the extra price.

items.prompt: Explain why age may matter for Ema’s cycle sizing and where it is insufficient. Fictional Ema Cycles makes smaller cycles for younger riders and larger sizes for adults. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Age segmentation groups customers by age where life stage or practical needs affect demand. Children’s and adult sizes can differ, but age does not establish every preference or income level. Use a meaningful product link and evidence instead of stereotypes. A buyer may also purchase on behalf of another age group. Size and safe fit provide a relevant age-related distinction, while price and style still need evidence from riders and purchasing adults.

items.prompt: Explain how Nela could assess a gender-based range without treating every customer alike. Fictional Nela Tailoring tests demand for different clothing cuts, asking customers about fit rather than assuming all preferences from gender. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Gender segmentation groups demand by gender where evidence shows a relevant difference in needs or preferences. It is one possible basis, not an assumption that every product must have separate male and female versions. Many needs are shared and individuals vary within categories. Choose fit, intended use or actual preferences when those explain demand better. Gender-related ranges may help where fit evidence supports them, but actual measurements and preferences remain important. A tool’s function may be better segmented by purpose instead.

items.prompt: Distinguish between market orientation and product orientation in the two design sequences. Fictional Hela Bottles surveys users about size before designing a bottle. Another invented producer builds its preferred technical design first and then looks for buyers. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Market orientation means research identifies customer wants before the product is developed and produced. Product orientation starts from the product or the enterprise’s technical strengths and then seeks buyers for that offering. The distinction is what guides the offering first, not whether either business advertises. Market focus can reduce the risk of an unwanted offer but costs time and research can be imperfect. Product focus can support technical innovation and expertise, yet may miss what buyers can use or afford. A business can combine technical capability with customer evidence rather than ignoring one. Hela’s sequence is market oriented; the other is product led. Advertising after either decision does not change which information guided the design first.
marking_guidance: Difference: Market orientation means research identifies customer wants before the product is developed and produced.

items.prompt: Define market orientation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Market orientation is an approach in which market research finds consumer wants before the product is developed and produced. Customer evidence guides the offer, although the business must also assess cost and capability. Research may be inaccurate or needs may change, so continue to test the response.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Market orientation is an approach in which market research finds consumer wants before the product is developed and produced.

items.prompt: Define product orientation. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Product orientation starts from the product, technical capability or producer’s preferred design and seeks a market for it. It can support innovation and technical quality but risks producing something buyers do not want or cannot afford. It is not simply making a poor product or doing no promotion.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Product orientation starts from the product, technical capability or producer’s preferred design and seeks a market for it.

items.prompt:
Fictional Rena Lunches can supply one reliable weekday meal range. Interviews with nearby workers show demand for quick affordable lunches. Tourists request varied evening menus that Rena currently cannot prepare. The owner compares serving the local work-purpose segment with launching the preferred evening menu without further customer evidence.

a(i) State two ways Rena could identify customer needs. [2]
a(ii) State the starting focus of market orientation and product orientation. [2]
b State two ways a business can meet a stated customer need. [2]
c Explain why purpose is a useful segmentation basis for Rena. [6]
d Evaluate a customer-led weekday offer against launching the owner’s preferred evening menu. [8]
items.canonical_answer: a(i) Interviews and review of customer feedback. a(ii) Identified consumer wants lead market orientation; the producer’s product focus leads product orientation. b Adapt product features and provide suitable access or timing. c Workers’ short breaks create a quick affordable weekday need, while tourist evening meals have different timing and variety requirements. Purpose helps separate these needs and match Rena’s limited range rather than treat all meal buyers alike. d The weekday offer fits both evidence and capability. The evening menu could reach another market but requires variety Rena cannot currently provide and lacks sufficient evidence. Choose the weekday segment, test paid demand and review results. Customer interest alone is not proof of profitable orders.

items.canonical_answer: a Interviews identify quick affordable worker lunches. Rena can choose a feasible meal, price and convenient weekday collection arrangement, then review actual orders. Choose the worker segment while validating volumes and costs; do not stretch into an unsupported range merely because a different market exists. Reconsider if demand or capability changes.

items.prompt:
Fictional Tuli Bags can make durable tool bags. Evidence shows enough local tradespeople interested at a feasible price, while a fashion segment requires rapid design changes beyond current capability. It compares work-purpose targeting with fashion targeting. For part (b) only, reliable new evidence shows most local tradespeople will not pay the feasible price, so the previously sufficient work-purpose demand disappears. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Tuli’s target choice under the original evidence. [12]
b Evaluate that choice after the price evidence changes. Explain whether the original judgement holds. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Work-purpose segmentation is justified by specific functional needs, feasible-price interest and capability. Fashion targeting does not fit current design resources. Choose a monitored work-bag test rather than produce for everyone. b The changed willingness to pay removes the sufficiency condition. Do not proceed at the same scale merely because the product is durable. Investigate acceptable features, costs or other reachable buyers before committing. Fashion remains beyond capability, so the failure of one target does not automatically make that alternative suitable. Pause and revise the evidence-led offering; customer focus requires responding to the new finding.
